topics.title: sein & haben
topics.summary: The two verbs you cannot learn German without: identity with sein and possession with haben.
points: sein is irregular: ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie/Sie sind.
haben is also irregular: ich habe, du hast, er/sie/es hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie/Sie haben.
Use sein for identity, origin and states; use haben for possession and many past tenses.

example.de: Ich bin Student und habe eine kleine Wohnung.
example.en: I am a student and have a small flat.

topics.title: Regular Present Tense
topics.summary: One stem, six endings: the pattern behind most German verbs.
points: Remove -en from the infinitive to find the stem: wohnen → wohn-.
Add -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en for ich, du, er/sie/es, wir, ihr, sie/Sie.
Stems ending in -t or -d add an extra e: du arbeitest, er arbeitet.

example.de: Du wohnst in Berlin und arbeitest dort.
example.en: You live in Berlin and work there.

topics.title: Gender & Articles
topics.summary: Every German noun has a gender, and the article must agree with it.
points: The definite articles are der (masculine), die (feminine) and das (neuter).
The indefinite articles are ein (masculine/neuter) and eine (feminine).
Always learn a noun with its article and plural: der Tisch, die Tische.

example.de: Das ist ein Tisch, und das ist eine Tür.
example.en: That is a table, and that is a door.

topics.title: The Accusative Case
topics.summary: The case of the direct object: only the masculine article changes.
points: Masculine der becomes den; ein becomes einen in the accusative.
Feminine, neuter and plural articles do not change in the accusative.
Direct object pronouns are mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch, sie.

example.de: Ich sehe den Hund und kaufe einen Apfel.
example.en: I see the dog and buy an apple.

topics.title: Questions & Negation
topics.summary: Ask questions two ways and say no with nicht or kein.
points: W-questions start with the question word, then the verb: Wo wohnst du?
Yes/no questions start with the verb: Wohnst du in Berlin?
Use nicht for verbs, adjectives and specific nouns; use kein before indefinite nouns: Ich habe kein Auto.

example.de: Wohnst du in Berlin? – Nein, ich wohne nicht in Berlin.
example.en: Do you live in Berlin? – No, I do not live in Berlin.

topics.title: The Dative Case
topics.summary: The case of the indirect object and of many common verbs and prepositions.
points: Articles change to dem (masculine), der (feminine), dem (neuter) and den + -n (plural).
Indefinite articles become einem, einer, einem and plural keinen.
Dative pronouns: mir, dir, ihm, ihr, ihm, uns, euch, ihnen.

example.de: Ich helfe dem Kind und danke der Lehrerin.
example.en: I help the child and thank the teacher.

topics.title: The Perfekt
topics.summary: The normal spoken past: haben or sein plus past participle.
points: Most verbs use haben: Ich habe gelernt.
Verbs of movement and change of state use sein: Ich bin gefahren.
Regular participles are ge- + stem + -t; irregular verbs have their own forms: gesehen, gegessen.

example.de: Wir haben gestern einen Film gesehen und sind danach nach Hause gegangen.
example.en: We watched a film yesterday and then went home.

topics.title: Modal Verbs
topics.summary: Attitudes and obligations: can, must, may, want, should.
points: Modal verbs take the second position; the main verb goes to the end in the infinitive.
Ich must remember: ich muss, du musst, er muss — no ending in the first and third person singular.
können, müssen, dürfen, wollen, sollen and mögen each change the vowel in the singular.

example.de: Ich muss heute länger arbeiten, aber ich kann morgen frei nehmen.
example.en: I have to work longer today, but I can take tomorrow off.

topics.title: Subordinate Clauses
topics.summary: because, that, if and although — with the verb at the end.
points: Subordinating conjunctions send the conjugated verb to the final position: weil, dass, wenn, obwohl.
The comma before the clause is obligatory in German.
After the subordinate clause, the main clause starts with its verb: Weil es regnet, bleibe ich zu Hause.

example.de: Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Deutschland studieren möchte.
example.en: I am learning German because I want to study in Germany.

topics.title: Two-Way Prepositions
topics.summary: Where or where to? The case decides the meaning.
points: The nine two-way prepositions are an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor and zwischen.
Use the dative for position (Wo?) and the accusative for direction (Wohin?).
Verbs such as legen, stellen and setzen express movement and take the accusative.

example.de: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch, aber ich lege es auf den Tisch.
example.en: The book is lying on the table, but I put it onto the table.

topics.title: Relative Clauses
topics.summary: Add information about a noun without starting a new sentence.
points: The relative pronoun agrees with the noun in gender and number, but its case depends on its role in the clause.
The conjugated verb moves to the end of the relative clause.
Use wo for places and was after alles, nichts and etwas.

example.de: Das ist der Kollege, der mir geholfen hat.
example.en: That is the colleague who helped me.

topics.title: Konjunktiv II
topics.summary: Politeness, wishes and unreal situations.
points: The most useful forms are hätte, wäre, könnte and würde + infinitive.
Use Konjunktiv II to make requests sound less direct: Könnten Sie …?
Unreal conditions combine wenn + Konjunktiv II with a Konjunktiv II main clause.

example.de: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich mitkommen.
example.en: If I had time, I would come along.

topics.title: The Passive Voice
topics.summary: Focus on what happens rather than who does it.
points: Form the passive with werden + past participle: Die Rechnung wird bezahlt.
The agent can be added with von (people) or durch (means).
The passive is common in reports, instructions and formal writing.

example.de: Die Rechnung wird morgen vom Kunden bezahlt.
example.en: The invoice will be paid by the customer tomorrow.

topics.title: Connectors & Word Order
topics.summary: Link ideas and keep the verb in the right position.
points: Coordinating connectors (und, aber, oder, denn) do not change word order.
Adverbial connectors (deshalb, trotzdem, außerdem) occupy position one, so the verb comes second.
Subordinating connectors (weil, obwohl, dass) send the verb to the end.

example.de: Es regnet, trotzdem gehe ich spazieren, weil ich frische Luft brauche.
example.en: It is raining; nevertheless I am going for a walk because I need fresh air.

topics.title: Adjective Declension
topics.summary: Adjectives take endings that mirror the article.
points: After der/die/das, adjectives take -e in the nominative singular and -en in most other forms.
After ein/eine, the adjective often carries the gender signal: ein neuer Film, eine neue Wohnung.
Without an article, the adjective takes the strong ending: neuer Film, neue Wohnung.

example.de: Ich habe den neuen Film in der kleinen Wohnung gesehen.
example.en: I saw the new film in the small flat.

topics.title: Konjunktiv I & Reported Speech
topics.summary: Report what someone said without endorsing it.
points: Form Konjunktiv I from the infinitive stem: er komme, sie habe, er sei.
If a Konjunktiv I form is identical to the indicative, use Konjunktiv II to keep the distinction.
Reported speech is standard in news, academic writing and formal minutes.

example.de: Die Ministerin sagte, die Reform sei notwendig.
example.en: The minister said the reform was necessary.

topics.title: Nominalisation
topics.summary: Turn actions into nouns for a compact, formal style.
points: Verb infinitives become neuter nouns: das Lesen, das Rauchen.
Suffixes such as -ung, -heit and -keit form nouns from verbs and adjectives: die Entscheidung, die Freiheit.
Nominal style is dense but can hide the agent; use it deliberately, not automatically.

example.de: Die Durchführung des Projekts erforderte eine schnelle Entscheidung.
example.en: The implementation of the project required a quick decision.

topics.title: Participial Constructions
topics.summary: Compress relative clauses into phrases before the noun.
points: Present participle + adjective ending: die steigenden Kosten (costs that are rising).
Past participle + adjective ending: die betroffenen Personen (the people affected).
Extended attributes sit between the article and the noun and are typical of formal written German.

example.de: Die zu erledigenden Aufgaben sind im Anhang aufgeführt.
example.en: The tasks to be completed are listed in the appendix.

topics.title: Advanced Subordination
topics.summary: Precise relationships between ideas: time, manner, consequence and concession.
points: sobald = as soon as; während = while/whereas; sodass = so that; indem = by doing so.
Two-part connectors such as zwar … aber and nicht nur … sondern auch structure contrast.
Keep verb-final order even in long clauses, and avoid stacking more than two subordinate clauses.

example.de: Sobald die Ergebnisse vorliegen, informieren wir Sie, sodass Sie planen können.
example.en: As soon as the results are available, we will inform you so that you can plan.

topics.title: Verb–Preposition Combinations
topics.summary: Some verbs require a fixed preposition — and often a fixed case.
points: Learn the pair as a unit: warten auf + accusative, sich interessieren für + accusative, teilnehmen an + dative.
Ask about things with wo- compounds: Worauf wartest du?
Refer back with da- compounds: Ich warte darauf.

example.de: Ich interessiere mich für Sprachen und warte auf eine Antwort.
example.en: I am interested in languages and am waiting for an answer.

topics.title: Modal Particles
topics.summary: Small words that carry tone: doch, ja, halt, eben, wohl.
points: Particles do not change the truth of a sentence; they change the attitude.
doch often adds emphasis or gentle contradiction; ja signals shared knowledge; halt/eben signal inevitability.
They are typical of spoken German and should be used sparingly in formal writing.

example.de: Das ist ja interessant, aber es ist halt nicht ganz einfach.
example.en: That is interesting, but it is just not that simple.

topics.title: Concessive Structures
topics.summary: Concede a point while keeping your argument intact.
points: zwar … aber, obwohl, wenngleich and auch wenn express concession at different levels of formality.
Concession makes an argument more credible when it is specific, not decorative.
Follow a concession with a clear main claim, often introduced by jedoch or dennoch.

example.de: Zwar ist die Maßnahme teuer, jedoch langfristig wirtschaftlicher.
example.en: The measure is expensive, but it is more economical in the long term.

topics.title: Register & Style
topics.summary: The same content demands different language in a email, a report and a conversation.
points: Register involves vocabulary, sentence length, pronoun choice and degree of explicitness.
Formal German favours nominal style, passive voice and impersonal constructions.
Spoken German tolerates particles, ellipsis and shorter clauses; do not mix the two carelessly.

example.de: Wir bitten um eine Rückmeldung bis Freitag. / Melde dich bitte bis Freitag.
example.en: We request a response by Friday. / Please get back to me by Friday.

topics.title: Function Verb Phrases
topics.summary: Fixed noun–verb combinations that sound precise and professional.
points: Expressions such as zur Anwendung kommen, in Betracht ziehen and zur Verfügung stellen are common in formal German.
The verb carries little meaning; the noun carries the content.
They are useful in reports but can sound bureaucratic in everyday speech.

example.de: Wir werden Ihren Vorschlag in Betracht ziehen.
example.en: We will take your suggestion into consideration.

topics.title: Complex Attributes
topics.summary: Genitive chains and participial phrases: unpacking dense academic German.
points: Genitive attributes usually follow the noun: die Bedeutung des Fortschritts.
Participial attributes precede the noun and can be extended: die von der Kommission beschlossene Reform.
When reading, find the noun first, then attach the attributes step by step.

example.de: Die von der Kommission beschlossene Reform trat im Januar in Kraft.
example.en: The reform passed by the commission came into force in January.

topics.title: Subjunctive Nuance
topics.summary: Distance, irreality, politeness and speculation — all in one mood.
points: Konjunktiv I signals reported speech and neutrality; Konjunktiv II signals unreality or politeness.
The double infinitive and past subjunctive allow precise counterfactuals: hätte machen können.
In literary German, the subjunctive can create distance without explicit reporting verbs.

example.de: Hätte man früher gehandelt, hätte das vermieden werden können.
example.en: Had action been taken earlier, that could have been avoided.

topics.title: Marked Word Order
topics.summary: Move sentence parts for emphasis, contrast and rhythm.
points: German allows the first position to be filled by almost any element for emphasis.
Fronting an object or adverbial creates focus: Diesen Vorschlag halte ich für problematisch.
Ausklammerung moves elements to the end for clarity or suspense, but should not become a habit.

example.de: Nicht die Kosten sind das Problem, sondern die fehlende Zeit.
example.en: The costs are not the problem; the lack of time is.

topics.title: Regional Variation
topics.summary: Standard German is a spectrum, not a single voice.
points: Austrian German uses Jänner, Semmel and Sackerl where Germany uses Januar, Brötchen and Tüte.
Swiss German writes ss instead of ß and uses Velo for bicycle.
Regional forms are acceptable in context; consistency matters more than choosing a single variety.

example.de: Im Jänner kaufe ich am liebsten frische Semmeln.
example.en: In January I like to buy fresh rolls (Austrian usage).

topics.title: Literary Tenses
topics.summary: How German literature uses tense for distance and immediacy.
points: The Präteritum is the default narrative tense in written fiction.
The Plusquamperfekt establishes what happened before the narrative present.
The historical present can create immediacy, especially in summaries and dramatic passages.

example.de: Sie hatte das Haus verlassen, bevor der Regen begann.
example.en: She had left the house before the rain began.

topics.title: Precision & Connotation
topics.summary: Choosing the right word is a matter of meaning, tone and company.
points: Near-synonyms differ in connotation: günstig is neutral, billig can sound dismissive.
Collocations are conventional word pairings; eine Entscheidung treffen is natural, eine Entscheidung machen is not.
Precision is not the same as rarity: the best word is the one the reader expects or is pleasantly surprised by.

example.de: Die Entscheidung war schwierig, aber letztlich tragfähig.
example.en: The decision was difficult but ultimately sustainable.
